<reason>Side A built a durable comparative framework—incentive asymmetry, lateral spread, and the invisibility of omissions versus publicly contestable content—and answered every pressure point with labeled, direct responses. Side B's sharpest weapon was the symmetry attack (oversight is fallible for both omissions and falsehoods, so PRO cannot assume correction works only for its side), plus a legitimate burden argument that PRO never quantified actual reach. But B offered no magnitude evidence for its own harm either, relying on hypothetical misleading frameworks rather than demonstrated prevalence, while A's asymmetry mechanisms at least did comparative work. B's Dover example, introduced properly in response to A's pressure question, was honest and well-caveated, yet A's closing effectively flipped it into his own witness: visible falsehood leaves a trail outsiders can fight, while self-censorship erases its footprint and hollows out the very assessments meant to detect it. A's answer to the symmetry attack—external contestation (courts, ballots, parents) as a channel unavailable against omissions—largely held. A's crystallization ("which threat can be fought?") made the debate easier to decide; B's closing was crisp but ended mostly on burden denial rather than a positive reason that miseducation currently outranks silence.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5's symmetry challenge ("you cannot make institutions politically vulnerable when evaluating omissions and politically reliable when evaluating falsehoods") was the debate's most damaging single move, and A5.4/A5.2's response—visible content can be fought by outsiders through courts and ballots as Dover itself proves, while fear silences both the lesson and the test question that would expose it—was the decisive counter that preserved A's path to victory.</best_rebuttal>
